title: Fewest Replacements to Make an Anagram

concept.title: Count the letters that are missing
body: In one step you may replace **any one letter** of the first word by any other letter. You want the first word to become an anagram of the second one (same letters, any order), using the fewest steps. A replacement changes the count of one letter down and the count of another up. So the minimum number of steps is the total amount by which the first word has **too few** copies of some letters: `sum(max(0, count_t[ch] - count_s[ch]))`.
The words have the same length, so the total surplus equals the total shortage: one replacement fixes one missing letter by using up one surplus letter. Counting shortages is enough.

statement: Two words `s` and `t` of the same length are given. In one step you may replace any letter of `s` by any other letter. Print the smallest number of steps that turn `s` into an anagram of `t`.
outputFormat: Print the smallest number of steps.
constraints: Both words have the same length and contain lowercase letters.

examples.note: Replace one b by an a.

hints: Count the letters of both words.
A letter is missing in `s` when `t` has more copies of it.
Add up the missing copies over all letters.

starter.python:
s = input().strip()
t = input().strip()

# Your code here

explanation: Each step can fix at most one missing letter, and every missing copy needs a step, so the answer is the total number of missing copies.

code.python:
s = input().strip()
t = input().strip()

cs = [0] * 26
ct = [0] * 26
for ch in s:
    cs[ord(ch) - ord("a")] += 1
for ch in t:
    ct[ord(ch) - ord("a")] += 1
print(sum(max(0, ct[i] - cs[i]) for i in range(26)))
